user_input: Right after the autoscaler added pods to the fraud detection service, payment authorizations started timing out. Only requests routed to the new pods fail, the older pods answer in under 300 ms. Is this a known problem, and how do we stop it from happening on every scale-up?
ground_truth_diagnosis: This is the documented cold-start incident (PM-2026-04). Newly scaled FraudDetectionService pods load their ML model lazily on the first scoring request and run on a cold JVM, so their first requests take several seconds, while PaymentGateway waits at most 2000 ms. The readiness probe only checked that the HTTP server was up, so Kubernetes sent traffic to pods that could not yet answer within the deadline. The fix is to load the model at startup and make readiness pass only after warm-up.

user_input: Right after AuthService rotated its signing keys, users who were already logged in started getting 401 on every request from the gateway, even though their tokens are less than an hour old. People who log in fresh are fine. What went wrong with the rotation?
ground_truth_diagnosis: AuthService removed the previous signing key from its JWKS at the moment of rotation. Access tokens stay valid for up to 1 hour, so already logged-in users still hold tokens signed with the old key, which the gateway can no longer verify and therefore rejects with HTTP 401, while fresh logins use the new key and work. This matches the documented 'old key removed before tokens expired' pattern.

expected_evidence_mapping.claim: Access tokens are valid for 3600 seconds (1 hour), so tokens signed with the old key outlive its removal.
Removing the previous key from the JWKS at rotation makes still-valid tokens unverifiable; the old key must stay published for at least the maximum token lifetime.
